title: Alternative Grading, Faculty Needs, and Trust
author: Robert Talbert
summary: Robert Talbert, now director of a teaching and learning center at a large flagship university, reflects on why alternative grading has been slow to take root among faculty there. He proposes a pyramid of professional needs for faculty, parallel to Maslow’s, running from material needs and safety through belonging and esteem to self-actualization, with uninterrupted time as a central need and trust as the connective tissue between levels. Alternative grading is built on trust in students, while traditional grading is built on compliance, so faculty who adopt it extend trust they often do not receive from a low-trust institution. He argues that institutions must meet the basic material needs, that teaching centers and departments should build trust and safe spaces for experimentation, and that faculty can form small learning communities. He cautions that conditions need not be perfect to start, but that trust and basic needs are as important to implementation as the idea itself.
points: Faculty have a hierarchy of professional needs, and a person worried about wages, contracts or promotion criteria has little capacity to redesign grading.
Trust is the connective tissue between each level of the pyramid, and when it fails at one level it infects the level above.
Alternative grading asks faculty to extend trust to students in an institution that does not extend it to them, creating an island of high trust in a low-trust environment.
Teaching centers can offer confidential consultations and faculty learning communities, and chairs have a critical role in giving faculty room to do their best work.
quotes: faculty have a hierarchy of professional needs, just like how Abraham Maslow taught us that all humans have a hierarchy of personal needs.
Time is the scarcest and most valuable resource faculty have. If you don’t have it, good luck reaching any of the levels above.
When trust breaks down at any level, it infects the level above it. If you don’t feel safe in your workplace, you will struggle to have any sense of belonging.
Alternative grading is, at its heart, based on trust. This a big part of what makes it deeply countercultural in higher education today — and why it can be so hard to adopt.

It is built on the mistaken belief that students won’t learn unless they are audited, with every action quantified by points and fed into a system intended to reduce them to a number and then deduce students’ learning from that number.

They are creating an island of high-trust culture when the institution around them is low-trust. Asking a faculty member to adopt a high-trust grading model means asking them to give away something they don’t receive.
the best thing it can provide is a safe space for faculty to come, learn, practice, make mistakes, and get feedback on their teaching. It’s a mirror image of a classroom focused on feedback loops.
the basic preconditions of trust and other fundamental needs are just as important to implementing an idea as the idea itself.
